what_its_for: Idursulfase is used to treat Hunter syndrome (also called Mucopolysaccharidosis II or MPS II). This is a rare inherited disease where your body cannot break down certain sugars called glycosaminoglycans. These sugars build up in your body and cause damage to organs and tissues. This medicine helps replace a missing enzyme called iduronate-2-sulfatase to help your body break down these sugars properly.
how_to_take: Idursulfase is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly injected into your vein through a needle or IV line. You will receive this medicine at a clinic, hospital, or infusion center under the supervision of a trained healthcare provider. Do NOT try to give this medicine to yourself at home unless your doctor has specifically trained you and approved it. Each infusion usually takes about 3 hours, but your nurse may slow it down or speed it up based on how you are feeling.
dosing: The usual dose for adults and children is 0.5 mg per kilogram of body weight, given once every week. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose based on your weight. Do not change your dose on your own. Always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss your weekly infusion appointment, contact your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to skip doses because consistent weekly treatment is important for this medicine to work properly. Do not try to double up doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Idursulfase is stored and handled by your healthcare team or pharmacy. It must be kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should NOT be frozen. Once the medicine is mixed and ready for your infusion, it should be used within 3 hours. You do not need to worry about storing this medicine at home in most cases.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all your medicines, vitamins, and supplements before starting treatment. Avoid skipping your weekly infusion appointments, as this can reduce how well the medicine works. Let your nurse know right away during your infusion if you feel unwell, have trouble breathing, feel flushed, or notice swelling, as these could be signs of an allergic reaction called an infusion reaction.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following during or after your infusion: difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, chest tightness or pain, throat swelling, hives or skin rash, flushing or redness of the skin, nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain, dizziness or feeling faint, fever or chills, swelling of the face, lips, or tongue. Also call your doctor if you notice any new or worsening symptoms of Hunter syndrome, or if you think you might be pregnant.
when_it_works: Idursulfase does not cure Hunter syndrome, but it can help slow the progression of the disease and improve some symptoms. Some patients may notice improvements in walking ability, breathing, and reduction of organ swelling over several months of regular treatment. Results vary from person to person. It is important to keep all your weekly appointments even if you do not feel immediate changes, as the medicine works gradually over time.
special_populations: Children: Idursulfase has been studied and used in children as young as 16 months old and is approved for pediatric patients. The dose is still based on body weight. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: There is very limited information about the safety of idursulfase during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding so your doctor can discuss the risks and benefits with you. Kidney or liver problems: Talk to your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect your care plan. Hunter syndrome primarily affects males, but females who are carriers should also discuss any health concerns with their doctor.
